title: Can Pop-Up Debate Produce Grit in Students?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart publishes the full text of his Character Lab teacher innovation grant application, which proposes testing whether pop-up debate can build grit rather than merely speaking skill. The design is the value here. Three weeks of Daily Facts establish why speaking, argumentation, content retention and grit matter strategically and personally, processed through writing and Frank Lyman's think-pair-share, which also normalizes public speaking before any debate happens because fear is the biggest barrier to a working pop-up. Then come twelve world history debates, each carrying a Target Skill and a paired Grit Tip kept on separate notebook pages, with students reflecting immediately after and again within 24 hours of watching themselves on film. Video is his answer to the missing ingredient in their growth: students believe they have poise until footage shows them their own verbal tics, and unvarnished feedback is what deliberate practice requires. His theory of why this should work is unusually candid - pop-up debate is hard enough to guarantee failure for every student, top to bottom, and that failure is the fertile soil the Grit Tips need. He closes with the indicators he would accept as success, including exit-slip evidence that students are rehearsing at home, and with the obstacles he expects, from speaking fear to parents refusing film releases.
points: The hypothesis is that a debate can serve as a petri dish for grit, not just for argument - a claim Stuart proposes to test with filmed evidence rather than assert.
The sequencing is the transferable part: three weeks of think-pair-share to normalize public speaking before Debate 1, because fear is the biggest barrier to a working pop-up debate.
Pairing each debate with both a Target Skill and a Grit Tip, each on its own notebook page, gives students something to execute and something to practice at the same time.
Video is justified as deliberate practice with a 24 Hour Rule, on the grounds that students who know Palmer's Poise element still have no idea how often they say 'like, um, uh, you know.'

He designs the task to produce failure on purpose - hard enough that even the highest achievers fall short - because grit instruction needs something real to be gritty about, and he sets a transfer test: exit-slip evidence of students rehearsing outside his room.
quotes: My project will center around a series of 12 in-class “pop-up debates,” the final 10 of which will be filmed and uploaded as “link-only” files on YouTube for immediate student review. While I’ve already observed that these debates help students with content retention, speaking/listening skills, and argumentative ability, my hypothesis with this project is that debates can serve as a petri dish for grit as well.

It’s worth noting that the initial three weeks of T-P-S will also serve to normalize public speaking [1] (the S mode involves me randomly calling upon students for their now-rehearsed thoughts), thus helping to overcome one of the biggest barriers to having great pop-up debates: fear.

The key (unstated) objective for this debate is simple: I want kids to experience that standing up and speaking in front of their peers does not result in death; it’s scary, but not impossible. Nervousness isn’t cured, but it’s put in its place.

However, my hunch is that their growth is retarded by the simple fact that they aren't allowed immediate, adequate feedback on their performances. For example, they know that Palmer's Poise element involves removing distracting behaviors and verbal tics from one's speaking; however, many of them simply have no clue how guilty they still are at using “like, um, uh, you know” repetitively when they speak.

Video can solve this — everyone who has ever watched themselves on film shudders because it's brutal, unvarnished feedback. This is a critical component of deliberate practice, and deliberate practice is basically the thing that builds skill.

It requires mastering of content, attending to speech delivery, listening well, processing quickly, organizing one’s thinking, and being brave. In other words, it will serve as a source of consistent failure for all of my students, from lowest- to highest-achieving. This failure will provide fertile soil for the Grit Tips, which will be designed for immediate application.

I have three years experience with scaffolding students toward successfully participating in Debate 1. The first debate is a pivotal moment, as students learn, “Hey, I can do this; it’s nerve-wracking, but I can do it.” Of the 200 students I’ve taught in the past three years, exactly one has refused to participate.
